title: Grace perfects nature
hookLine: Aquinas: grace doesn't destroy what's human but completes it

cards: A wedding in a village called Cana, and in the middle of the feast the wine runs out. Jesus tells the servants to fill the stone jars with water and take some to the man running the feast.

He tastes it, and it's wine, and he calls the groom over, puzzled: "thou hast kept the good wine until now." Notice what Jesus didn't do. He didn't cancel the party, or swap the wedding for a prayer meeting.
He took plain water, the stuff of an ordinary day, and made it better than anyone expected. Thomas Aquinas has a short line that fits that pattern.

teach.b: Near the start of his Summa, Aquinas asks whether reason has any place in sacred teaching.
His answer turns on a short phrase: grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it. Grace here means God's own gift, given freely.

Nature means what we are as creatures: bodies, minds, appetites, friendships, the ability to think. Aquinas's point is that God's gift doesn't come to wipe all that out and start over. It comes to finish it.
So reason isn't faith's enemy; it can serve faith. The same pattern runs through his whole picture of a human life.
Courage, fairness, self-control: good human strengths, and grace doesn't cancel them. It lifts them toward faith, hope and love.
Paul's letter to Timothy points the same way: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving."

Christians weigh this differently. Catholic teaching draws on Aquinas's line. Lutheran and Reformed teaching stresses how deeply sin has wounded human nature, so that grace must heal before it can complete.
Orthodox Christians speak of human beings being drawn into God's own life. Aquinas also says grace heals a nature wounded by sin, but his emphasis falls on completion.
In his picture, grace doesn't take a person out of being human. It finishes the work.

how: Catholic teaching quotes Aquinas's line that grace perfects nature; Christians of different churches give thanks for food, work, friendship and beauty as good gifts of God.

s: Aquinas taught that grace replaces human nature with something else

games.q: a friend says: to be truly holy, give up everything natural, music, good food, friends. you're Aquinas. what do you say?
o: agree: the natural is the enemy of grace.
say grace doesn't destroy nature but completes it.
games.why: Aquinas says grace does not destroy nature but perfects it. like the water at Cana, the ordinary is made better, not thrown out.

practice: Choose one ordinary good within reach: the taste of what you're drinking, sunlight on your hands, a song you love, the warmth of a blanket. Give it your full attention, without hurrying past it to something more spiritual.
If you pray, receive it with thanksgiving, the way Paul's letter puts it; if you don't, simply let yourself enjoy it.

wordCard.voice: Grace perfects nature. Aquinas's line: God's gift doesn't destroy what's human, but completes it, the way water at Cana became good wine.
